clinicalPearls: Usually autosomal dominant, caused by variants in THRB encoding the beta isoform of the thyroid hormone receptor
The characteristic biochemistry is raised free thyroxine and free triiodothyronine with a non-suppressed (normal or mildly elevated) TSH
Most patients are clinically euthyroid because the reduced sensitivity is broadly compensated by higher hormone levels
Tissue-specific effects can occur: tachycardia and hyperactivity may reflect the intact beta receptor pathway in some tissues alongside resistance in others
Goitre, learning difficulties, and attention problems are recognised associations, particularly in children
The main differential is a TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma, which also causes high thyroid hormones with unsuppressed TSH
Most patients need no treatment; the priority is to avoid inappropriate antithyroid therapy or thyroidectomy for a misdiagnosis of hyperthyroidism
reference.pathophysiology: Thyroid hormone acts through nuclear receptors, of which the beta isoform predominates in the pituitary and liver and mediates negative feedback on TSH secretion. Dominant-negative variants in THRB produce a receptor that binds hormone or DNA poorly yet interferes with the normal receptor, so target tissues expressing the beta receptor are relatively resistant. Because pituitary feedback is blunted, TSH secretion is not suppressed despite high circulating thyroid hormones, and the raised hormone levels represent the compensation needed to achieve near-normal action in resistant tissues. Tissues that rely more on the alpha receptor, such as the heart, remain sensitive and may show features of hormone excess, giving the mixed clinical picture. The persistently non-suppressed TSH is the diagnostic clue that distinguishes the condition from primary hyperthyroidism.
additionalInvestigations: Free thyroxine and free triiodothyronine with a simultaneous non-suppressed TSH
Repeat and confirmatory thyroid function tests to exclude assay artefact
Alpha-subunit measurement and dynamic testing to distinguish from a TSH-secreting adenoma
Pituitary MRI where a TSH-secreting tumour cannot be excluded biochemically
Assessment of peripheral markers of thyroid hormone action such as sex hormone-binding globulin
redFlags: Symptomatic tachyarrhythmia such as atrial fibrillation
Growth or neurodevelopmental concerns in an affected child
Pituitary mass on imaging suggesting a TSH-secreting adenoma instead
Inadvertent thyroid ablation or antithyroid treatment for misdiagnosed hyperthyroidism
reference.prognosis: Most individuals have a normal life expectancy and remain well without treatment; the principal risk is iatrogenic harm from misdiagnosis, while a minority have persistent cardiac or neurodevelopmental symptoms requiring targeted management.
pitfalls: Treating the raised thyroid hormones as hyperthyroidism and giving antithyroid drugs or thyroidectomy
Failing to distinguish the condition from a TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma
Overlooking assay interference as a simpler explanation for discordant results
Not screening first-degree relatives for the dominant condition
references: OMIM entry for resistance to thyroid hormone beta
management: Most patients are compensated and euthyroid and require no thyroid-directed treatment, so the priority is avoiding iatrogenic harm from inappropriate antithyroid drugs, radioiodine or thyroidectomy
Securely distinguish the condition from a TSH-secreting pituitary adenoma before any intervention, using dynamic testing, alpha-subunit measurement and pituitary imaging
Beta-adrenergic blockade to control tachycardia and adrenergic symptoms arising from tissues that remain hormone-sensitive
Recognise and support learning difficulties and attention problems, particularly in affected children
Periodic monitoring of goitre, cardiac status and peripheral markers of thyroid hormone action
Genetic counselling for autosomal dominant THRB disease with cascade family testing to prevent misdiagnosis in relatives
